_comment: The game's palette, taken from tiles2 rather than from the generator. tiles2 re-tints its whole tileset to the HUD's muted-forest theme via postprocess.palette (grass and dirt are colours the DESIGNER supplied); an earlier tiles 3.0 palette was measured from what PixelLab happens to produce, which is the generator's average and not an art direction at all. That is why 3.0 grass came out a bright yellow-green (#64b84d, hue 107deg) against 2.0's deep pine (hue 166deg) — 90 luminance apart. Values here are tiles2's ACTUAL APPEARANCE, not its configured target: 2.0 harmonises hue/sat while keeping each pixel's own value, so its art lands well above its target, and a flat 3.0 top has to match what the eye sees.

_wall_comment: The colour a material has as a WALL, which is NOT its top colour. The maintainer spotted that grass under an ice tile did not match grass under a grass tile: the same material was coming out four different greens depending on which cell drew it (hue 72-119, value 71-113). A wall needs one target per material, and it cannot simply be the top colour — a vertical face is lit differently, and the ratio is not even constant across materials (measured: grass 1.38x its top value, ice 0.70x). So hue and saturation come from the palette, and the VALUE is the median of what the generator actually draws for that material as a wall.

slime__over__grass.note: 'The grass is not colored to our grass in this image' - every tile in the set measures wall_err 39-46 against the gate of 30, so the grass wall shipped RAW in the generator's olive-yellow instead of our deep green. Same override the maintainer sanctioned for deep water: the wall material is not in question here, only its drawn colour. Olive share 0.21 -> 0.00.

dark_mud__over__slime.note: 'The left slime wall is light brown redish? Bottom left wall should be green.' The darker-lit LEFT wall face sits closer to the mud anchor than to slime's own wall, so the split hands it over - 16 of 17 rows wrongly brown, against a correct 6-row brim on the right face. fix_left_wall.reclaim_left_wall converts only the body: the brim depth is measured per column on the RIGHT face and protected on the left, and the bottom row of each column stays brown. It repaints nothing - the converted pixels take a colour already in the tile, rank-matched and rescaled to the face's own brightness. APPLIED DIRECTLY to the published art, never via a publish run: publish.py no longer reproduces the committed slime (a fresh run turns vivid mint 49,189,117 into olive 94,138,46 with no tweak at all), and slime is PROTECTED.

deep_water__over__grass.note: 'I have painted RED on the overhang that should be deep_water, but currently is green/grass. I also marked in purple what should be grass so you don't take too much.' The generator draws the water droop on BOTH faces - the prompt asks for it - but the wall split measured every drape against an anchor taken on the fully lit TOP face, so on the shaded left face the water read as far from its own material and was handed to grass: 90% of the drawn water kept on the right face, 5% on the left. relight_faces scales that anchor to each face's own lighting, read off the side material because it is the one thing drawn on both faces, and only where the palette confirms it really is the side material - this cell's left drape covers 74% of its face, so an unfiltered median would measure the WATER and call the face bright. Result: left 5% -> 94%, right unchanged, and ZERO grass pixels claimed, which is the purple half of the instruction. OPT-IN, because refereed library-wide on a lighting-invariant hue metric it is a wash that makes left/right asymmetry worse (7.8% -> 9.8%, 42 tiles better and 29 worse).

deep_water__over__slime.note: 'RED = the lower part of the left wall and should be slime. YELLOW = the upper parts of the left wall is currently deep_water and should continue to be deep water.' Measured: the left wall is DRAWN 4-8% water and shipped 95-99% of it. The flood is not the culprit here and neither are the anchors - the colour test alone calls 95-98% of that wall water, and it is not wrong to be confused: shaded slime is (28,61,30) against a water top face of (43,72,74), while the same slime on the lit face is (78,132,65). Relighting the anchors per face was tried and fixed one tile of five. So this is the pair claim_depth exists for - 'for the pairs colour cannot decide... the tweak is geometric'. 0.40 keeps the top 40% of the wall as the drape and returns the rest to slime, which is exactly the yellow/red line drawn. Swept 0.30-0.50; the right face, which was never complained about, moves by at most 2 points at this setting.

grass__over__black_rock.note: 'Grass over black rock has an issue where the green overhang is grey' - three tiles sent, all with grey patches in the green drape near the lip. Diagnosed per axis on the pixels that ship grey: they are plainly green in the art (21,84,62) and the split calls them rock 100% of the time, because the grass anchor is measured on the LIT TOP FACE at value 159 while the drape hangs on a shaded wall at 83, with the rock anchor at 43 - the drape lands nearer the rock, 6.30 against 10.08. Every whitening weight is pinned at WHITEN_STD_FLOOR here, so the metric is not the problem: the anchor is standing in the sunshine. drape_lit relights it to the drape's own lighting (selected by hue, which black rock cannot contaminate because it has none); relight_faces then corrects the shaded face against the lit one. Measured over all 45 candidates: grass kept 94% -> 100%, worst tile 60% -> 98%, and rock wrongly claimed stays at ZERO px. claim_lip was tried first and rejected - it buys 4 points by greening up to 48 rock pixels a tile.

grey_stone__over__dark_mud.note: 'The grey stone overhang to the left (looks like a border) is brown.' Measured over all 17 candidates: of the stone actually drawn in that border band, only 76% survived, and on the worst tiles the left face kept 13-16%. This pair is the case claim_lip exists for and the reason is measurable: BOTH materials are achromatic in the art - stone is saturation 4 and the mud only 9 - so nothing in the colour plane separates them and only value is left, and on the shaded left face the drape sits at 82 with mud at 32 and the stone top at 134. Dead even, 50 against 52. The claim is 3 rows because that is what the generator draws: median drape depth 3 on both faces. Result: border 76% -> 100%, for 7 wrongly claimed mud px per tile (max 11). relight_faces and drape_lit were both measured here first and rejected - they buy deeper drips the maintainer did not ask about and over-claim up to 348 px of mud.

_transition_comment: transition_surface is the maintainer's taxonomy (2026-08-21), set after reviewing all 17 composed pairs. 'own' keeps the generated transition art with hue/sat corrected to the palette and the pixel's relief carried through - his verdict on the grass pages: 'A calm base texture is better than a clean color, but they have to be very very subtile'. And near a boundary it SHOULD differ from the field: 'grass near a road usually is different'. 'base' copies the material's base tile into its region so the transition mimics its neighbour - paving and parquet, where the generator's freehand stones read wrong beside the laid field. 'flat' fills the top with the single palette colour, wall texture kept - the declared fallback 'when we have still not found that perfect texture', and probably permanent for lava/water/deep_water, which the game animates instead. A material may later carry several base_tiles; a field then draws them interchangeably to kill repetition.
_LAW_no_repetition: NEVER INTRODUCE A TOP TEXTURE. A flat top stays flat. Texture on the ground arrives ONE way only: the maintainer promotes a base tile. No agent decides a surface should carry texture, no matter how good the individual tile looks, because a good tile repeated is still repetition and repetition is the thing he cannot stand. His words, 2026-08-21: 'YOU CAN NEVER TAKE DECISION TO BRING IN A TOP TEXTURE. DONT EVER BRING IN REPETITION AGAIN.' This has now been learned three times in one day - mixing 15 different grass sets per cell, rolling pure cells across pool sets, and prototyping a textured matrix top - so it is written here rather than remembered. transition_surface 'own' is NOT an exception: it keeps texture the generator already drew INSIDE a transition tile, where each tile is unique and nothing repeats. It never applies to a field.
